reference: An entity must register for GST when the following two requirements are satisfied (s 23-5):The entity carries on an ‘enterprise’The entity’s GST turnover is over the ‘registration turnover threshold’ An entity may register for GST if they carry on an enterprise but do not meet or exceed the registration turnover threshold.Topic 15, Goods and services tax, Lecture Slide Pg. 5

They may also register for GST if they meet the turnover threshold but do not carry on an enterprise. Neither of these gains are discount capital gains or eligible for small business concessions. What is his net capital gain that must be included in his assessable income? Option A: $20,000 Option B: $16,000 Option C: $ 38,000 Option D: $22,000 Option E: None of the above The correct answer is Option D.
reference: 20,000 - 10,000 = 10,000 (CG to be included in assessable income) 10,000 + 6,000 (Net capital loss brought forward from last year) = 16,000 (Net Capital Gain) Note: Capital losses can be applied against capital gains to reduce the overall taxable capital gain. reference: 1- Promoting financial stability by leading institutions to manage risk prudently for minimizing losses to depositors, policy holders etc. - This is the core objective of the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC). 2- Developing a conceptual framework - The AASB develops conceptual frameworks for the purpose of accounting for transactions and events. 3- Contributing for developing a single set of accounting standards for global use - The AASB works towards achieving this objective through its involvement in the International Accounting Standards Board (IASB). 4- Formulating accounting standard that consist of law under s.334 of the Corporations Act - The power to formulate accounting standards is vested in the AASB by s.227(1) of the ASIC Act. 5- Uplifting the significance of main objects of the financial reporting system part of the ASIC Act - The main object of the financial reporting system is to assist in the economic decision making process.The above are the functions of the AASB under s.227 of the ASIC Act, except for point 1 as it is the core objective of the ASIC. Reference: Topic 3 - Source of income (Slide 4)   Mr. Chugh is a resident of India, who comes to Australia to work for a while. He enters into an agreement with a French company to do some work in France for six months. He goes to France and completes the work. The income he receives from the French company for the work he does in France will be income derived in France and will be taxable in France. As a temporary resident of France he would be required to pay tax at the prevailing French rates. If he were a resident of France he would be entitled to the tax-free allowance. He would not be required to pay Australian tax on this income. He would, however, be required to pay Australian tax on any income he received from Australian sources. If he has not been a resident of Australia for more than 183 days he will not be entitled to the tax-free allowance. If he has been a resident of Australia for more than 183 days he will be entitled to the tax-free allowance on his ordinary income. He will still not be required to pay Australian tax on the income he received from French sources. The High Court held that the expenditure was not a capital expenses and allowed the deduction. The Commissioner allowed the deduction as the expenditure was incurred in making an item functionally better rather than its restoration. The High Court held that the expenditure was capital expenditure and not allowed for income producing purpose. The court held that the expenditure was an improvement and not a repair. reference: Chapter 18 Trading Stock – Page # 18.3 – Trading stock during the year. input: Given question: Which characteristic is not a part of taxation law legislation? Option A: Interpreted based on the doctrine of precedent Option B: Measure net gains and losses over a period Option C: ]Some receipts not recognised for tax law purpose example:gifts one off or unusual receipts Option D: Expenses are immediately deductible while capital out goings are deductible over time The correct answer is Option B.
reference: be used to overcome the deficiencies in the legislation. It helps in filling the legislative vacuums. Judicial precedent, also known as stare decisis, is the principle that courts should follow their own previous decisions. This allows for consistent interpretation and application of the law. Taxation law is no exception to this principle. It is interpreted based on the doctrine of precedent. This means that judicial precedent is an important source of tax law. Legislation may be incomplete or ambiguous. In such cases, the courts can refer to the legislative history, which includes things like the reports of parliamentary committees, to help fill legislative vacuums. This process of interpreting legislation involves consideration of a number of factors, including the words of the legislation, the purposes behind it and the intended beneficiaries. When interpreting legislation, the courts often look at the purpose behind it. They do this by considering the words of the legislation in the context of the problem it was designed to address. They also consider the intended beneficiaries of the legislation. Reference is taken from chapter- 1 ,Research design and methodology, Taxation principles and theory. It is therefore essential that the legislation is interpreted based on the doctrine of precedent to ensure that taxpayers can rely on the law. Tax law recognises the value of money and therefore provides that expenses are immediately deductible while capital outgoings are deductible over time. This is because capital outgoings are spread over a period of time to ensure that the taxpayer is not disadvantaged by having to pay tax on the cost of a capital item in the year in which it is acquired.Gains and losses are generally computed by comparing the amount with the taxpayer’s “cost” of the CGT asset. This is called the “cost base” of the CGT asset. Some receipts not recognised for tax law purpose such as gifts, one off or unusual receipts are not included in assessable income. reference: 236001FBTAA Fringe Benefit Tax Assessment Act 1986 s136(1) provides the general rules for calculating the taxable amount of a fringe benefit. The taxable amount is calculated as follows:Taxable Amount = (Fringe Benefits Taxable Value x FBT Rate) - FBT Exemption Amount Taxable Value of Fringe BenefitThe taxable value of a fringe benefit is determined under s 136(2). If the fringe benefit is a car fringe benefit, the taxable value is further calculated under Div 10 FBTAA. Employer's FBT LiabilityEmployer's FBT liability is calculated under s 146 FBTAA. It is calculated as follows:Employer's FBT Liability = (Total Fringe Benefit Cost x FBT Rate) - FBT Exemption Amount  Under s 147(1), if an employer elects to use the cost basis for a car fringe benefit, the cost is determined according to the rules in Div 10. instruction: As an explanation generation expert, can you generate the explanation for the given input?
input: Given question: Which of the following requirements are necessary to met for an extraordinary or isolated transaction to satisfy the first strand of Myer? Option A: there was a business operation or commercial transactionthere was a profit making intention upon entering the transactionthe profit was made by the means of consistent with the original intention Option B: only 1 Option C: 1 and 3 Option D: 1, 2 and 3 Option E: none of the above The correct answer is Option D.
reference: 1 there was a business operation or commercial transaction2 there was a profit making intention upon entering the transaction3 the profit was made by the means of consistent with the original intention4 Extraordinary transactions are those which are outside the ordinary course of business and isolate transactions are those where the taxpayer has not previously undertaken such a transaction and does not intend to do so in the future. Therefore, option D is correct. Reference: Foundation of Taxation Law, 9th edition, 2017, Stephen Barkoczy, page 384-385, topic 14, Provision that deny or limit deductions, 1st strand of Myer.
